speakerBio: Lead of the hospital's inpatient diabetes service who has spent a decade trying to abolish correction-only insulin one ward at a time.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

Ward round, day 3. A 66-year-old man admitted with cellulitis and type 2 diabetes has a glucose chart that reads like a rollercoaster: 4.1, then 19.8, then 5.2, then 22.1. His prescription? A "sliding scale" of subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin given only when the glucose is already high — and nothing else. His usual basal insulin was stopped on admission "to be safe". He feels awful, his wound is not healing, and the nurses are chasing his sugars all day and all night. Nobody is out of their depth clinically — but the system he has been put on is guaranteed to produce exactly these swings. This lecture is about why inpatient glucose matters, what to aim for, and why reactive "correction-only" insulin is one of the most persistent bad habits in hospital medicine.

1 · 🩺 Why inpatient glucose matters

Hyperglycaemia in hospital is not a cosmetic number on a chart — it is independently associated with worse outcomes: more wound and surgical-site infections, impaired neutrophil function and immunity, poorer wound healing, longer length of stay, more ICU admissions, and higher mortality across medical and surgical cohorts. But the correction is not "drive the glucose to normal at all costs" — the NICE-SUGAR trial (NEJM 2009) showed that intensive control (target 4.5–6.0) in the critically ill increased mortality compared with a conventional target (≤10), driven by hypoglycaemia. So both ends of the range harm. The goal is a sensible middle.

In the hospital, both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia kill — the art is to sit safely between them, not to chase a perfect number.

2 · 🎯 The targets

Guidelines (JBDS-IP, ADA inpatient standards) converge on a pragmatic range for most non-critically-ill inpatients:

GroupTarget glucoseNote
Most non-critical inpatients~6–10 mmol/L (acceptable up to 12)The JBDS working range — avoids both extremes
Critically ill (ICU)Insulin usually started >10; target ~6–10 (≤10)Per ADA/NICE-SUGAR — avoid intensive 4.5–6 targets
Frail / end-of-life / high hypo riskRelaxed (e.g. 6–12+, avoid lows)Prioritise avoiding hypoglycaemia
Any inpatientAvoid <4 mmol/LHypoglycaemia is the outcome to fear most acutely
💡 6 to 10 is the number

For most ward patients, aim for a glucose of 6–10 mmol/L (tolerating up to ~12). Below 6 you are creeping towards hypoglycaemia; above 12 you are into the harm zone for infection and healing. Chasing 4–6 on a general ward is how you cause hypos.

3 · ⚖️ The central contrast — basal-bolus vs "sliding-scale-only"

The single most important message of this lecture. A physiological insulin regimen mimics the pancreas: a basal component covering background hepatic glucose output, a prandial (bolus) component for meals, and a small correction component for excursions. "Sliding scale" — subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin given only in response to an already-high glucose, with no basal and no meal cover — throws away two-thirds of that physiology.

Scheduled BASAL-BOLUS (correct)Sliding-scale / correction-ONLY (poor)
DesignBasal + meal-time bolus + correction — proactive, physiologicalRapid-acting insulin only when glucose already high — reactive
TimingAnticipates the glucose riseAlways chasing a rise that already happened
Glucose patternSmoother, in-range more oftenSaw-tooth swings — hyper, over-correct, hypo, rebound
Basal coverAlways present (essential in T1DM)Absent — dangerous in type 1 (DKA risk)
EvidenceRABBIT-2 (Diabetes Care 2007): basal-bolus beat sliding-scale in T2DM inpatientsAssociated with more hyper- and hypoglycaemia
⚠️ Why correction-only insulin is intrinsically bad

It is reactive, not proactive: it does nothing until the glucose is already high, then gives a dose, which often over-shoots into a hypo, which is over-treated, producing a rebound high — the classic saw-tooth. It provides no background insulin, so in type 1 diabetes it invites ketoacidosis. The landmark RABBIT-2 trial showed a scheduled basal-bolus regimen achieved markedly better glucose control than sliding-scale alone in general-medicine and surgical type 2 inpatients. A correction scale is fine as an add-on to scheduled insulin — never as the whole regimen.

A sliding scale on its own doesn't control diabetes — it documents it, one high reading at a time.

4 · 🧮 How to run a proper subcutaneous regimen

For the insulin-requiring inpatient who is eating:

  • Continue basal insulin (never stop it in type 1). Estimate total daily dose (TDD) if starting fresh — roughly 0.3–0.5 units/kg/day, lower in the elderly/renal impairment; split ~50% basal, ~50% divided across meals.
  • Prandial (bolus) rapid-acting insulin with each meal; hold or reduce if not eating.
  • Correction doses added to the meal-time bolus for readings above target — a supplement, not the whole plan.
  • Review daily and titrate to the pattern (fasting high → adjust basal; post-meal high → adjust that bolus).

5 · 💧 The variable-rate intravenous insulin infusion (VRIII)

The VRIII (the modern replacement for the term "sliding scale" when it means an IV insulin infusion) is for patients who cannot use a subcutaneous regimen. Run it correctly and it is safe; run it wrong and it causes hypos, hypokalaemia, and ketoacidosis.

When is a VRIII indicated?

  • Type 1 or insulin-treated type 2 who are nil by mouth or not eating/absorbing reliably and cannot be managed with adjusted subcutaneous insulin.
  • Vomiting / not tolerating oral intake, or acute illness with poor control.
  • Prolonged fasting for surgery/procedures (session 12).
  • DKA/HHS use fixed-rate protocols, which are distinct.

How to run it — the JBDS rules

RuleWhy
Always run a substrate fluid alongside (e.g. 0.45% saline with 5% glucose ± potassium, or 5–10% glucose)The insulin needs glucose to act on — infusing insulin without substrate causes hypoglycaemia and ketosis
NEVER stop the patient's basal (long-acting) insulin in type 1 diabetes — continue it alongside the VRIII (often at reduced dose)Stopping basal leaves no insulin cover if the VRIII is interrupted → rapid ketoacidosis
Monitor capillary glucose hourly and titrate the insulin rate to a scaleTo keep glucose 6–10 and catch hypos early
Monitor potassium (at least daily; more if abnormal) and include K in the substrate fluidInsulin drives K into cells → hypokalaemia
Check ketones / venous bicarbonate if glucose rising despite infusionDetect evolving DKA (esp. if basal stopped or line failed)
Plan the exit early — convert back to SC insulin with overlapStop the VRIII only after the first SC dose is on board (overlap ~30–60 min) or you'll rebound
⚠️ The two classic VRIII killers

(1) Stopping the long-acting basal insulin in a type 1 patient "because they're on the drip" — if the IV line tissues or the pump stops, they have zero insulin and go into DKA within hours. Keep the basal running. (2) Running insulin with no glucose substrate — guaranteed hypoglycaemia. And always watch the potassium.

💡 The overlap rule when stopping a VRIII

Because IV insulin has a half-life of only a few minutes, if you stop the infusion before subcutaneous insulin has taken effect the patient is briefly uncovered and rebounds high (or into DKA). Give the first SC dose, wait 30–60 minutes with the infusion still running, THEN stop the VRIII.

6 · 💊 Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia — mechanism & the daily pattern

Glucocorticoids cause hyperglycaemia by increasing hepatic gluconeogenesis, inducing peripheral insulin resistance, and impairing insulin secretion. The clinically vital point is the time-course, which tracks the drug. Once-daily morning prednisolone peaks in its glucose-raising effect in the afternoon and evening, then wanes overnight.

🎯 The steroid glucose fingerprint

Morning prednisolone → morning fasting glucose is often normal, but glucose climbs through the afternoon and evening. This is why a fasting-only glucose check misses it — you must monitor after lunch and in the evening. It also dictates the treatment: match the insulin to the steroid's profile.

  • Preferred approach: morning intermediate-acting insulin (e.g. isophane/NPH) given with the steroid — its action peaks in the afternoon, mirroring the steroid's glucose rise, and wanes overnight to reduce nocturnal hypo risk.
  • For patients already on insulin, up-titrate daytime/lunchtime and evening doses; add correction.
  • Monitor pre-lunch, pre-evening-meal and pre-bed, not just fasting.
  • As the steroid dose tapers, taper the insulin in parallel to avoid hypos.

7 · 🍽️ Feed-related hyperglycaemia

Artificial feeding delivers carbohydrate in a pattern the usual insulin regimen was never designed for.

FeedGlucose problemInsulin approach
Continuous enteral (NG/PEG) feedSteady carbohydrate load over the feeding periodMatch with intermediate/long-acting insulin over the feed; if feed stops abruptly, hypo risk — have glucose ready
Bolus enteral feedsMeal-like spikesRapid-acting insulin with each bolus feed
Parenteral nutrition (TPN)High continuous glucose infusion → hyperglycaemiaInsulin added to the TPN bag or a separate VRIII; monitor closely
⚠️ When the feed stops, the insulin doesn't

If a continuous feed is interrupted (tube blocked, feed held for a procedure, patient pulls the NG out) but the matched insulin is already given, the patient will drop into hypoglycaemia. Whenever feed is held, check glucose and have a glucose infusion available; align insulin timing to the feed.

8 · 🔌 Insulin pumps (CSII) in hospital

Patients on continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion pumps are usually expert in their own diabetes. The default is to let a competent, conscious patient continue self-managing their pump, with a local pump policy, documentation, and diabetes team involvement.

  • Continue the pump if the patient is alert, competent, and able to manage it.
  • Remove/stop the pump and switch to a VRIII or basal-bolus if: the patient is critically ill, has DKA, is unconscious/unable to manage it, is having imaging that requires removal (MRI/CT with the device in field), or the site is failing. Ensure background insulin is provided when the pump comes off.
  • Involve the inpatient diabetes team early.

9 · 🛡️ Hospital hypoglycaemia prevention

Iatrogenic inpatient hypoglycaemia is a measurable safety event with its own prevention bundle:

  • A nurse-led hypoglycaemia treatment protocol on every ward (fast carb → recheck 15 min → repeat → long-acting carb; IV glucose if unable to swallow).
  • Prescribe hypo treatment proactively for every insulin/sulfonylurea patient on admission.
  • Right-size targets (6–10, relaxed in frailty), review insulin daily, and reduce doses when intake falls or illness resolves.
  • Never use correction-only insulin as the sole regimen; avoid stacking correction doses.
  • Flag high-risk patients (CKD, prior severe hypo, unawareness, long fasts) and align insulin to feeds/steroids.
☠️ M&M — the sliding-scale rollercoaster

A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on basal insulin at home was admitted with cellulitis. On arrival a junior stopped his basal insulin "to avoid hypos" and wrote a subcutaneous sliding scale of rapid-acting insulin, correction-only. Over 72 hours his glucose swung between 3.6 and 23: each high was over-corrected into a hypo, each hypo over-treated with juice into a rebound high. He developed ketonaemia (no basal insulin cover), his cellulitis failed to improve, and on day 4 he had a symptomatic hypo of 2.9 while a subsequent reading of 24 triggered a large correction dose that dropped him again. The inpatient diabetes team, called late, switched him to a scheduled basal-bolus regimen with a correction supplement; his glucose settled into 6–10 within a day and his wound began to heal. Lessons: (1) correction-only insulin is reactive and produces saw-tooth swings and ketosis — RABBIT-2 showed basal-bolus is superior; (2) never stop basal insulin to 'prevent hypos' — it causes ketosis and worse swings; (3) a correction scale belongs on top of scheduled insulin, not instead of it; (4) early referral to the diabetes team fixes exactly this. The team treated each glucose reading in isolation instead of prescribing a physiological regimen.

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Inpatient glucose matters — hyperglycaemia worsens infection, healing, and mortality, but intensive control harms too (NICE-SUGAR); aim for the middle.
  2. Target ~6–10 mmol/L for most ward patients (up to 12 acceptable; avoid <4); relax in frailty.
  3. Use scheduled basal-bolus, not correction-only insulin. Sliding-scale-alone is reactive and causes saw-tooth swings and (in T1DM) ketosis — RABBIT-2 favours basal-bolus. A correction scale is an add-on, never the whole plan.
  4. Run a VRIII properly: always with substrate glucose, never stop the basal insulin in type 1, monitor glucose hourly and potassium daily, and overlap SC insulin before stopping.
  5. Steroid hyperglycaemia peaks in the afternoon/evening after morning prednisolone — monitor post-lunch/evening and use morning intermediate insulin; taper insulin as steroids taper.
  6. Match insulin to feeds and beware the hypo when a feed stops; let competent patients keep their insulin pumps unless critically ill/DKA/unable.

moderatorQs.q: Contrast a scheduled basal-bolus regimen with sliding-scale-only insulin. Why is the latter poor, and what evidence supports basal-bolus?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: A basal-bolus regimen mimics the pancreas: background basal insulin for hepatic glucose output, prandial bolus insulin for meals, and a small correction supplement — it's proactive and keeps glucose smooth and in range. Sliding-scale-only gives rapid-acting insulin only once the glucose is already high, with no basal and no meal cover. It is intrinsically reactive: it does nothing until the glucose has risen, then often over-corrects into a hypo that gets over-treated into a rebound high — the classic saw-tooth. Worse, the absence of basal insulin invites ketoacidosis in type 1 diabetes. The RABBIT-2 trial (Diabetes Care 2007) showed a scheduled basal-bolus regimen achieved significantly better glucose control than sliding-scale alone in type 2 inpatients. A correction scale is legitimate only as an add-on to scheduled insulin, never as the entire regimen.

moderatorQs.q: What are the essential safety rules for running a VRIII?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Five rules. (1) Always run a substrate fluid (glucose-containing, e.g. 0.45% saline/5% glucose ± potassium) alongside — insulin with no glucose to act on causes hypoglycaemia and ketosis. (2) Never stop the patient's long-acting basal insulin in type 1 diabetes — keep it running (often reduced) so that if the line fails they still have cover; stopping it risks DKA within hours. (3) Monitor capillary glucose hourly and titrate the rate to keep glucose ~6–10. (4) Monitor potassium and include it in the substrate fluid, because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and causes hypokalaemia. (5) Plan the exit — when converting back to subcutaneous insulin, give the first SC dose and overlap it with the infusion for 30–60 minutes before stopping, because IV insulin's half-life is only minutes and stopping early causes rebound hyperglycaemia or DKA.

moderatorQs.q: A patient on morning prednisolone has normal fasting glucose but you suspect steroid hyperglycaemia. Explain the pattern and how you'd manage it.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Glucocorticoids raise glucose by increasing hepatic gluconeogenesis, causing peripheral insulin resistance, and impairing insulin secretion — and the effect tracks the drug's pharmacokinetics. Once-daily morning prednisolone produces a characteristic pattern: the fasting/morning glucose is often normal, but glucose climbs through the afternoon and evening and falls overnight. So fasting-only monitoring misses it — you must check pre-lunch, pre-evening-meal and pre-bed. Management mirrors the profile: give morning intermediate-acting insulin (isophane/NPH) with the steroid so its peak matches the afternoon glucose rise and wanes overnight to limit nocturnal hypos; up-titrate daytime doses in those already on insulin. Critically, as the steroid dose tapers, taper the insulin in parallel to avoid hypoglycaemia.

audienceQs.q: On admission should I just stop a type 2 patient's home insulin and put them on a sliding scale?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — that's the habit we're trying to break. Stopping the home insulin and using a correction-only sliding scale removes background cover and produces exactly the hyper–hypo swings (and, in type 1, ketosis) you're trying to avoid. If the patient is eating, continue their basal insulin, keep meal-time doses, and add a correction supplement for excursions — a scheduled basal-bolus. Only switch to a VRIII if they genuinely can't manage a subcutaneous regimen (nil by mouth, vomiting, not absorbing, acutely ill). Aim for a glucose of 6–10 mmol/L, review the chart daily, and call the inpatient diabetes team if it's not settling.

audienceQs.q: A patient on a continuous NG feed and matched insulin just had their feed stopped for a scan. What should I watch for?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Hypoglycaemia. The insulin was dosed to cover the carbohydrate in the feed, so once the feed stops but the insulin is already on board, the glucose can drop. Whenever a continuous feed is interrupted — for a scan, a blocked tube, or the patient pulling it out — check the capillary glucose promptly and then regularly, and have a glucose (dextrose) infusion available to run in place of the feed if needed. Flag it to the team so the insulin can be adjusted or a substrate infusion started, and try to align any planned feed breaks with the insulin timing. The same caution applies to bolus feeds and TPN.

audienceQs.q: A well type 1 patient on an insulin pump is admitted with a fractured wrist. Do we take the pump off?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Not if they can manage it. The default is to let a competent, alert patient continue self-managing their own pump, under a local pump policy, with clear documentation of basal rates and boluses and early involvement of the inpatient diabetes team. You'd only remove the pump and switch to a VRIII or basal-bolus if the patient becomes critically ill, develops DKA, is unable to operate the pump (reduced consciousness, sedation, confusion), needs imaging requiring device removal, or the infusion site fails — and whenever the pump comes off you must ensure background insulin is provided so they're never left without cover. A fractured wrist in an otherwise well, competent patient is not a reason to take over their diabetes.
